title: Reading and inspecting data
summary: Load a CSV and get to know it before you trust it.

steps.title: read_csv
body: Most data arrives as a file. `pd.read_csv` reads one into a DataFrame, guessing a dtype for
each column. It accepts a path, a URL, or any file-like object; in this course the data is
inline text wrapped in `io.StringIO`, which behaves like an open file:
```python
import io
import pandas as pd
text = """product,qty,price
Widget,3,2.50
Gadget,1,10.00
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))
# in real life: pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
The first line becomes the column names. Numbers become `int64` / `float64`, text becomes
`str`.

steps.explain: An empty cell becomes NaN, and because NaN is a float, `score` is `float64`. Text columns are pandas 3's `str` dtype.

steps.title: First look: head, info, describe
body: Before any analysis, look at the data:
```python fragment
df.head()          # first 5 rows (df.tail() for the last)
df.shape           # how big
df.dtypes          # did every column get the type you expected?
df.info()          # dtypes + non-null counts + memory, in one view
df.describe()      # count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max of numeric columns
df["region"].unique()   # the distinct values of a column
Surprises show up here: a numeric column read as `str` (a stray `"n/a"`), far fewer non-null
values than rows, a max of `9999` that is really a missing-value code.

steps.prompt: Which one call shows each column's dtype **and** how many non-missing values it has?
steps.explain: `describe()` summarises numbers (its `count` row is non-missing values, but only for numeric columns). `info()` covers every column.

steps.prompt: You want to know... which do you call?
pairs: what the first rows look like
the mean and quartiles of numeric columns

steps.title: read_csv options you will need
body: Not every file is a tidy comma-separated one. The options that fix most of them:
```python fragment
pd.read_csv(f, sep=";")                 # semicolon-separated (common in Europe)
pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", decimal=",")    # and 3,5 means 3.5
pd.read_csv(f, na_values=["n/a", "-"])  # extra strings that mean "missing"
pd.read_csv(f, usecols=["a", "b"])      # only load some columns
pd.read_csv(f, index_col="id")          # use a column as the row index
pd.read_csv(f, dtype={"zip": str})      # keep leading zeros in codes
Fixing a problem while reading is cheaper than cleaning it up afterwards.

code: df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text), sep=";", decimal=",", na_values=["n/a"], index_col="id")
steps.explain: `index_col` moves `id` out of the columns into the index, so 2 columns remain. `decimal=","` and `na_values` make `rain` a clean float column.

steps.prompt: Summarise the numeric columns and find gaps.
steps.explain: `describe()` has a row per statistic; `isna().sum()` counts missing values per column: `[0, 1]`.

steps.title: Profile a dataset
prompt: Write `profile(text)` that reads a comma-separated CSV string and returns a dict:
"numeric": ["age", "score"],        # numeric column names, in file order
"missing": {"score": 1},           # only columns with at least one missing value
Use `df.select_dtypes("number")` for the numeric columns and `df.isna().sum()` for the gaps.
steps.starter:
import io
import pandas as pd


def profile(text):
    df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))
solution: "missing": {col: int(n) for col, n in gaps.items() if n > 0},
hints: `{col: int(n) for col, n in df.isna().sum().items() if n > 0}`
